title: Marie Curie's Life In Reverse | From a Nobel Grave to a Warsaw Classroom
description:
Marie Curie's life runs backwards in this episode, from her death in a French mountain sanatorium in 1934 back to her birth in a Warsaw classroom in 1867. The journey steps through her two Nobel Prizes, the tonnes of pitchblende residue boiled down in a leaking shed, the X-ray cars she drove toward the front in the First World War, and the freezing room in the Latin Quarter where she first counted her own francs. Every scene moves to an earlier year, so the discoveries arrive in reverse order and the costs behind them become visible. Dates, places and measurements follow the documented record of her life.

scenes.narration: In Paris today, two of Marie Curie's laboratory notebooks are kept in a lead-lined box, because they are still radioactive more than a century after she wrote in them. Her ashes rest inside the Pantheon, the monument that holds France's great figures. In 1995 her remains and Pierre's were carried there, and she became the first woman admitted on her own achievements.

Sixty-one years before that ceremony, on July 4, 1934, Marie Curie died at the Sancellemoz sanatorium at Passy in the French Alps, of aplastic anemia, a condition that had stopped her blood from forming. She was sixty-six years old. She was buried beside Pierre at Sceaux, outside Paris. A year later her daughter Irene and son-in-law Frederic Joliot-Curie received the chemistry prize.

The end came after a long decline. Through the winter of 1933 and 1934 her strength faded, and doctors found her white blood cells dangerously low. She had handled radioactive material for decades without protection, and the damage had been accumulating. In the spring of 1934 she travelled to the mountain sanatorium, hoping the quiet and the clean air would restore her. They did not.

Thirteen years earlier, in May 1921, she boarded a ship for the United States. American journalists had raised money to buy her a gram of radium, far beyond what her laboratory could afford. President Warren Harding handed it to her at the White House. She toured the country for a month, collecting further gifts for her institutes in Paris and in Warsaw.

Seven years before that, during the First World War between 1914 and 1918, she fitted out a fleet of cars with X-ray equipment and drove them toward the field hospitals herself. People called them the little Curies. She learned to change a tyre and to jump-start an engine, and she taught women operators to hold a plate steady under a wound in the dark.

By 1916 the effort had grown far beyond a few cars. She organised permanent X-ray rooms behind the front lines and kept the mobile units moving between dressing stations. Her teenage daughter Irene worked beside her as an operator. Accounts of the service credit it with examining more than a million wounded soldiers before the armistice, so that surgeons could see before they cut.

Before the war, in 1914, the Institut du Radium opened on a new campus in Paris with Marie Curie in charge of its laboratory. The building kept radioactive samples on one side and delicate instruments on the other. When the German army approached that autumn, she packed the radium into lead boxes and sent it west. The work resumed as soon as the line held.

In December 1911, the Royal Swedish Academy awarded her the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on its own, for the discovery of radium and polonium and for the work of isolating radium. It was the first time one person had won a second Nobel Prize. She had shared the physics prize eight years earlier. The chemistry prize, for her country's new element, was hers alone.

Ten weeks before that announcement, in October 1911, she had sat among seventeen physicists at the first Solvay Conference in Brussels, a meeting funded by a Belgian industrialist to argue over the nature of matter. Einstein was in the room. She was the only woman there, and the discussion of atoms and quanta ran through several long days of argument.

Nine months before that, in January 1911, the French Academy of Sciences had voted on a new member and turned her candidacy down. No woman had ever been elected to that body, and the French press reported the ballot as a test of whether the rule would bend. It did not bend. She returned to her lecture hall and to the measurements waiting in her laboratory.

In 1910, working with her colleague Andre Debierne, she pushed the work a step further and produced a sample of pure radium metal, a grey material that glows faintly and stays warm to the touch. She also fixed the element's atomic weight more precisely. The sample showed that radium belonged on the periodic table beside the older elements, with a number of its own.

In November 1906, five months after Pierre's death, the Sorbonne offered her his chair. She stood in the same lecture hall where he had taught and picked up his course at the exact sentence where he had left it. She was the first woman to hold a professorship at that university, and she kept teaching the subject the two of them had built together.

Five months earlier, in June 1906, Pierre had been killed on a Paris street. He stepped out of a building on the rue Dauphine and was struck by a heavy horse-drawn wagon, and he died soon afterwards. He was forty-six. The couple had worked side by side on radioactive material for a decade, and Marie was left to run their laboratory alone.

In December 1903 the Royal Swedish Academy gave the Nobel Prize in Physics to Henri Becquerel and to the Curies for their joint research on radiation. When the first nomination named only Becquerel and Pierre, Pierre wrote to the committee and insisted that Marie be included. She became the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize, at the age of thirty-six.

Six months before that, in June 1903, she had defended her doctoral thesis at the Sorbonne on the radioactive substances she and Pierre had isolated, tested with instruments she had helped to build. The examiners passed her. For years the practical work had taken place in a converted shed with a glass roof, where the rain came through in bad weather.

Two years before that, in 1902, she had turned a warehouse problem into a chemical one. From several tonnes of pitchblende residue shipped from a mine at Joachimsthal in Bohemia, she drew out a tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride and weighed it carefully to set radium's atomic weight. The figure she published became the reference number for the new element.

In December 1898 she and Pierre announced a second new element in the journal of the French Academy, and named it radium after the Latin word for ray. The claim rested on a spectral line that no other laboratory had seen and on a reading of activity far stronger than uranium could produce. Proof by weight was still three years away.

Five months before that, in July 1898, the same journal had carried their report of a first new element, which she called polonium after her native Poland, then ruled from St Petersburg. The name was a quiet political act as much as a chemical one. Its activity was many times stronger than uranium's, measured with an electrometer that Pierre had designed.

Behind both announcements stood the hardest work of all. Through 1898 she and Pierre boiled and stirred kilograms of pitchblende residue in a converted shed, heating dishes over stoves, a process that would take four years to finish. They moved the heavy material by hand, and the air inside the shed stayed thick with vapour through the summer and the winter.

In September 1897, in the middle of that campaign, the Curies' first daughter, Irene, was born in Paris. Her parents arranged the laboratory hours around her, and the child grew up among glassware and notebooks. Irene trained as a physicist in turn, and in 1935 she received a Nobel Prize of her own, one year after her mother's death.

Two years earlier, in July 1895, Marie Sklodowska had married Pierre Curie at the town hall in Sceaux, south of Paris. They were both physicists. She wore a dark blue dress instead of white, and they spent the wedding journey cycling through the countryside. She was twenty-seven, and the marriage gave her a laboratory partner for the rest of her working life.

The meeting had come a year before that, in the spring of 1894, while she was finishing a study of how steel behaves in a magnetic field. A Polish physicist who knew them both introduced her to Pierre Curie, who was already publishing on crystals and on magnetism. They argued about measurements first, then about the possibility of sharing a laboratory.

A year earlier, in 1893, she had completed her degree in physics at the Sorbonne, and in 1894 a second degree in mathematics. She had arrived in Paris in 1891 with savings from a governess's wage. The university took women in theory, but in the examination halls they were still expected to beat the men sitting around them.

Three years before that, in 1891, she had taken a small room in the Latin Quarter and enrolled at the Sorbonne as Maria Sklodowska. The room was unheated, and in winter the water froze in the washbasin. She counted every franc, sometimes choosing a new book over a meal, and she worked late in the reading rooms of the city libraries.

For much of the previous decade she had worked as a governess in the Polish countryside, teaching the children of landowners. The wage was small, and she sent part of it to her sister Bronislaw, who was studying medicine in Paris. The plan was a bargain between sisters: Bronislaw would finish first, then send money so that Marie could follow.

Before that, in 1883, at the age of fifteen, she had finished her schooling in Warsaw. Poland was then ruled from St Petersburg, and a girl who wanted a university degree had nowhere at home to take it. The faculties were closed to women, and the nearest open doors were in France, a country she had never seen and could not yet afford to reach.

Five years earlier, in 1878, tuberculosis had taken her mother after a long illness at home. Maria was ten years old, the youngest of five children, and her father, a teacher of mathematics and physics, was left to raise the household. The disease moved quietly through the rooms, and for years the family had listened to it through the walls.

Two years before that, in 1876, her eldest sister Zofia had died of typhus, in a house full of children still at school. Fevers moved fast between crowded rooms in Warsaw, and no one in the family was spared the fear of them. The household carried on, quieter than before, with one chair at the table left empty.

The story began on November 7, 1867, in Warsaw, when Maria Sklodowska was born, the youngest of five children in a household of teachers. Her father taught mathematics and physics and kept instruments at home. The city was under Russian rule, and the family's language, their ambitions and their schoolwork were all carried on under watch.
